label: Riemannian Submanifolds
notes: This chapter, spanning printed pages 225 through 262, studies how a submanifold inherits geometry from its ambient space. We split the ambient connection into tangent and normal parts, package the bending into the second fundamental form, and read off the Gauss and Codazzi equations that culminate in the Theorema Egregium.

label: The Setup
notes: We fix an isometric immersion of a manifold into a Riemannian ambient space, giving each point a tangent space and an orthogonal normal space. The induced metric makes the submanifold Riemannian, and the orthogonal splitting of ambient vectors along the submanifold is the engine that drives every formula in this chapter.

label: The Gauss Formula
notes: Covariantly differentiating two tangent fields with the ambient connection yields a vector that need not stay tangent. Projecting it splits the derivative into the induced tangential connection plus a normal correction. That decomposition is the Gauss formula, and its normal part is exactly the second fundamental form we study next.

label: The Second Fundamental Form
notes: The second fundamental form is the symmetric, normal-valued bilinear map measuring how the submanifold curves away from its tangent plane inside the ambient space. Symmetry follows from torsion-freeness of both connections, and bilinearity over functions makes it a genuine tensor rather than a differential operator depending on extensions.

label: The Shape Operator
notes: Fixing a unit normal converts the normal-valued second fundamental form into a self-adjoint endomorphism of the tangent space, the shape operator or Weingarten map. The Weingarten equation gives it as the tangential derivative of the normal field, and self-adjointness guarantees real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigendirections everywhere.

label: Principal Curvatures
notes: Because the shape operator is self-adjoint, the spectral theorem supplies orthonormal principal directions with real principal curvatures. These eigenvalues record the extreme normal curvatures of curves through the point, and every normal curvature lies between the smallest and largest principal value, a fact Euler's formula makes precise.

label: Mean and Gaussian Curvature
notes: Two symmetric functions of the principal curvatures matter most. The mean curvature is their average, the trace of the shape operator, governing minimal surfaces. The Gaussian curvature is their product, the determinant, and the chapter's main surprise is that this extrinsic-looking product is secretly intrinsic.

label: The Gauss Equation
notes: The Gauss equation expresses the ambient curvature tensor restricted to tangent vectors in terms of the submanifold's own curvature plus quadratic terms in the second fundamental form. It cleanly separates intrinsic curvature from the extrinsic bending, letting us compute sectional curvatures of the submanifold from ambient data and the shape operator.

label: The Codazzi Equation
notes: The Codazzi equation captures the normal component of the ambient curvature, equating it with the covariant derivative of the second fundamental form taken antisymmetrically. When the ambient space has constant curvature this normal component vanishes, forcing the second fundamental form to be a Codazzi tensor, a strong integrability constraint on hypersurfaces.

label: Hypersurfaces
notes: For a hypersurface there is a single unit normal up to sign, so one shape operator and one second fundamental form carry all extrinsic information. The Gauss equation then reduces to a product formula: sectional curvature in a principal two-plane is the product of the two principal curvatures spanning it.

label: Theorema Egregium
notes: Gauss's remarkable theorem follows as a corollary: for a surface in Euclidean space the Gaussian curvature, defined as the product of principal curvatures, equals the intrinsic sectional curvature. Bending a surface without stretching preserves curvature, so a flat plane can never be wrapped onto a sphere without distortion.

label: Synthesis
notes: The chapter's architecture is one orthogonal splitting unfolding into a tower of identities: Gauss formula, second fundamental form, shape operator, principal curvatures, and the Gauss and Codazzi equations. Their joint payoff is the Theorema Egregium, the bridge from extrinsic geometry to intrinsic invariants that opens the rest of the theory.
